## Packages and Data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(labelled)
library(gtsummary)
library(car)

theme_gtsummary_compact()   # smaller font and padding for slides

case31 <- read_sav("Case 31 Data_efcu_1_DM_cleaned.sav") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.labelled), as.numeric)) |>
  mutate(
    hq   = factor(q38, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No")),
    loan = factor(q27, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Yes", "No"))
  ) |>
  set_variable_labels(
    hq   = "Lives in headquarter area",
    loan = "Currently has a loan with the CU",
    q31  = "CU keeps information confidential",
    q32  = "CU loan processing is prompt",
    q33  = "CU meets members' needs",
    q34  = "CU loan applications are simple",
    q37r = "Overall rating of the CU",
    employee_proficiency_index = "Employee proficiency index"
  )
dim(case31)
```

::: aside
Data: Case 31, Employees Federal Credit Union (n = 128). Cleaned in my data preparation assignment.
:::

# Prompt 1: Capabilities of {gtsummary} {background-color="aquamarine" transition="fade"}

## The Prompt

> **In Step 1, you have seen how to create a summary table and modify it for various statistical analyses. Summarize the package's capabilities as explained by the speaker. How may the {gtsummary} benefit you for your school work or career?**

## What the Package Can Do

::: incremental
- **Table 1 summaries:** `tbl_summary()` guesses whether each variable is continuous, categorical, or dichotomous and reports median (IQR) or n (%) by default. It can be split with `by =`.
- **Cross-tabulations:** `tbl_cross()` builds crosstabs with row, column, or cell percents and margins, and `add_p()` adds the right test.
- **Group comparisons:** `add_p()`, `add_q()` (multiple-comparison correction), `add_overall()`, `add_n()`, and `add_difference()` add columns to a summary.
- **Models:** `tbl_regression()` summarizes a model with the right header (such as odds ratio) and finds reference rows; `tbl_uvregression()` runs a series of one-variable models.
- **Other data types:** `tbl_svysummary()` for survey data and `tbl_survfit()` for survival data.
- **Building and styling:** `tbl_merge()`, `tbl_stack()`, `tbl_strata()`, plus `modify_*()`, `bold_*()`, and `italicize_*()` functions.
- **Themes:** One line sets defaults for a journal, language, or compact layout.
:::

## How It Works: The Formula Syntax

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Left side of the formula **selects** variables, right side gives the **instruction**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
tbl_summary(
  data = case31,
  by = hq,
  label = q37r ~ "Overall rating",
  statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
  digits = all_continuous() ~ 2
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- `label = q37r ~ "..."` renames one variable.
- `all_continuous()` is a gtsummary selector, and tidyselect helpers like `starts_with()` also work.
- `"{mean} ({sd})"` is a glue string, so any function (even my own) can be used.
- Several instructions go in a `list()`.
:::
:::::

## Example: A Table 1 in Few Lines

```{r}
#| label: tbl-demo
#| tbl-cap: "Member ratings by headquarter-area residence"
case31 |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = hq,
    include = c(q31, q32, q33, q34, q37r),
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
    digits = all_continuous() ~ 2,
    missing = "no"
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  add_p(test = all_continuous() ~ "t.test") |>
  bold_labels() |>
  modify_spanning_header(all_stat_cols(stat_0 = FALSE) ~ "**Lives in HQ area**")
```

::: notes
Show that one pipe gives labels, n, mean (SD), an Overall column, and p-values. Without being told, the package picked up the variable labels I set earlier.
:::

## How It Can Help Me

. . .

**School work**

::: incremental
- Every assignment so far (data preparation, data analysis tables, now the CEP report) needs tables. `{gtsummary}` turns results into a formatted table without copying numbers by hand.
- Because tables come from code, they stay **reproducible**: if I fix a variable, I re-render and the table updates.
:::

. . .

**Career**

::: incremental
- As a digital marketing analyst I report survey and campaign results. Clean tables and `inline_text()` numbers make reports look professional and cut errors.
- Journal themes and Word output (via flextable) will help when I write the CEP report.
:::

# Prompt 2: Sjoberg's Extended Talk {background-color="aquamarine" transition="fade"}

## The Prompt (2.1)

> **In Step 2, you watched the extended presentation of the {gtsummary} package by Dr. Daniel Sjoberg, the very creator of the package. 2.1. How does it differ from gt and gtExtras?**

## 2.1 gtsummary vs. gt vs. gtExtras

| Package | What it is | Main job |
|:-----------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|
| **gt** | Posit's "grammar of tables" | Formats **any** data frame into a table: headers, spanners, footnotes, number formats, colors |
| **gtExtras** | Add-on for gt | Extra styling: ready-made themes (such as newspaper looks), sparklines, in-cell bars, icons, color helpers |
| **gtsummary** | Statistical summary package | **Computes** the statistics (summaries, tests, regression results) and then formats them. It uses gt behind the scenes |

. . .

- `gt` and `gtExtras` display numbers I already have. `gtsummary` calculates them from data or from a model object.
- `as_gt()` converts a gtsummary table to a gt object, so every gt (and gtExtras) function can still be used for extra polish [@sjoberg2021].

::: aside
gt provides the table engine; gtSummary provides the statistical content.
:::

## The Prompt (2.2)

> **2.2. Give three things you learned newly that were not explained in the lecture in Step 1.**

## 2.2 Three New Things I Learned

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**1. `inline_text()` puts table numbers in the report text.** I can write "the odds ratio for age is `r '`r inline_text(...)`'`" and the estimate, confidence interval, and p-value are pulled straight from the table object. A pattern argument controls the format, so the text can never disagree with the table.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**2. Print engines.** Tables print with `gt` by default, but gt's PDF and Word (RTF) output is still under construction. For Word, `flextable` is the backup (gtsummary uses it automatically in Word output if installed); `kable` is simplest; and `as_hux_table()` can produce raw LaTeX code. This matters because the CEP report may need Word.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
**3. Building blocks and helpers.** `add_q()` corrects p-values for multiple comparisons (and prints the exact `p.adjust` call so nothing is hidden), `show_header_names()` shows the hidden column names needed by `modify_header()`, and `add_stat()` adds any custom column. Even a custom table (a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel table) was built by combining `tbl_cross()`, `tbl_merge()`, `add_stat()`, and `tbl_stack()`. Models with no broom method can be used by supplying a `tidy_fun`.
:::

::: notes
Be ready to explain that the first item changes my workflow most: copying numbers from tables into sentences is where mistakes happen.
:::

# Prompt 3: Cross-Tabulation {background-color="aquamarine" transition="fade"}

## The Prompt

> **3. Apply what you learned to your MSDM CEP data. Choose two appropriate variables for cross-tabulation and show if the two variables are associated or not. Use appropriate statistics to test if the two variables are associated. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.**

::: callout-warning
## Data note

The CEP survey has not been fielded yet (the IRB review is pending), so I used the **Case 31** credit union data as a stand-in. The same code can be reused on the CEP data once it is collected.
:::

## Question and Variables

- **Research question:** Are members who live in the headquarter area less likely than members who live elsewhere to have a loan with the credit union?
- **Variables:** `hq` (lives in HQ area: yes/no) and `loan` (currently has a loan: yes/no)
- Both variables are nominal, so a **chi-square test of independence** fits.
- $H_0$: residence and loan status are independent. $H_A$: they are associated.

## Cross-Tabulation with `tbl_cross()`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross
#| tbl-cap: "Loan status by headquarter-area residence"
case31 |>
  tbl_cross(
    row = hq,
    col = loan,
    percent = "row",
    missing = "no"
  ) |>
  add_p(source_note = TRUE) |>
  bold_labels()
```

## Chi-Square Details

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
tab <- table(case31$hq, case31$loan)
chisq.test(tab)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$expected   # expected counts
fisher.test(tab)$p.value
```
:::
:::::

## Interpretation

::: callout-note
## Is residence associated with loan status?

- Among HQ-area members, **35%** have a loan; among members who live elsewhere, **54%** do.
- The 2×2 chi-square test with continuity correction (the default in `add_p()`) gives χ²(1, N = 128) = 3.62, *p* = .057. Without the correction, χ² = 4.34, *p* = .037, and Fisher's exact test gives *p* = .049.
- All expected counts are above 5, so the chi-square test is valid.
- The evidence is **borderline**: at α = .05, the test with correction does not reject independence, while the other two tests barely do. The odds ratio is about 0.47 and Cramér's V is about .18 (a small effect).
- I would say the data **suggest** HQ-area members are less likely to borrow from the credit union, but the result is not strong and should be confirmed with more data.
:::

# Prompt 4: Multiple Regression {background-color="aquamarine" transition="fade"}

## The Prompt

> **4. Using the MSDM CEP data, run multiple regression. The dependent variable can be continuous or dichotomous. Regress a dependent variable on a set of independent variables. Code, produce the table, and interpret the result.**

## Model

- **Dependent variable (continuous):** `q37r`, overall rating of the credit union (1 = Very Poor to 5 = Excellent)
- **Independent variables:** confidentiality (q31), promptness (q32), meeting needs (q33), simple applications (q34), employee proficiency index, and residence (`hq`)

```{r}
m1 <- lm(q37r ~ q31 + q32 + q33 + q34 + employee_proficiency_index + hq,
         data = case31)
```

## Regression Table with `tbl_regression()`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reg
#| tbl-cap: "OLS regression predicting overall rating of the credit union"
tbl_regression(
  m1,
  intercept = TRUE,
  estimate_fun = \(x) style_number(x, digits = 2)
) |>
  bold_p(t = 0.05) |>
  bold_labels() |>
  add_glance_source_note(include = c(r.squared, adj.r.squared, nobs))
```

## Checking Multicollinearity

```{r}
vif(m1)
```

All VIF values are below 1.6, so multicollinearity is not a concern.

## Interpretation

::: callout-note
## What predicts the overall rating?

- The model is significant, *F*(6, 114) = 11.96, *p* \< .001, and explains about **39%** of the variance (adjusted R² = .35, n = 121; 7 cases dropped because of missing q37r).
- **Employee proficiency** is the strongest predictor: a one-point higher index goes with a 0.42-point higher overall rating (*p* \< .001), holding the other variables constant.
- **Prompt loan processing** (b = 0.21, *p* = .014) and **meeting members' needs** (b = 0.20, *p* = .023) are also significant positive predictors.
- Confidentiality (b = 0.14, *p* = .122), simple applications (b = −0.05, *p* = .513), and residence (b = 0.18, *p* = .101) are not significant.
- **Practical meaning:** Members' overall rating depends most on how they see employees, speed, and whether needs are met. This is an association, not proof of cause.
:::

# Conclusion {background-color="#a13c65" transition="zoom"}

## Key Takeaways

::: incremental
- `{gtsummary}` calculates and formats tables in one pipeline, which saves time and reduces copy-paste errors.
- It differs from `gt` and `gtExtras` because it computes the statistics.
- Cross-tabulation: HQ-area members were less likely to have a loan, but the evidence is borderline.
- Regression: employee proficiency, promptness, and meeting needs predict overall rating.
:::
